original.description: Objective: The objective of the activity is to develop and test a thin optical aperture leveraging advances in integrated photonic technology to reduce the size andweight of space-based optical communication terminals.TargetedImprovements:Reduction of both size and weight of satellite laser communication terminals by 50%.Description: Optical communication terminal solutions with lower size and weight are required to serve the increasing role of small spacecraft for satellitecommercialisation by maximising the amountof payload space for mission-enabling processing or sensors. State-of-the-art optical communicationterminals are often too bulky and heavy for such small platforms and a leap in technology is required. This activity will seek innovative integrated photonicsolutions to replace the telescope subsystem of an optical communication terminal and eliminate as much as possible the need for free-space propagationinside the laser terminal. By doing so, it is expected to greatly reduce the size and inertial mass of the telescope subsystem, enabling for instance furtherreductions in steering assembly size, weight and power.This activity will design and prototype a photonic aperture (or flat telescope) that shall provide good beam quality (for coupling/emitting into/from singlemode waveguides such as single-mode fibres), shall be relatively large (at least several cm in diameter) or provide enough optical gain to enable convincingreplacement of conventional beam expansion and free-space propagation optics (traditional telescope assemblies) in space optical communicationterminals. A foundry-compatible fabrication process of the photonic aperture shall also provide a low-cost telescope alternative by eliminating the need forexpensive optics and assembly and alignment touch labour.The following tasks are envisioned:- Identify the potential solutions and latest innovations in integrated photonic able to replace conventional optical aperture assemblies in space-basedoptical communications for small platforms and/or use cases where accommodation of optical communication terminals is drastically constrained bytheir size and weight.- Develop a preliminary design and expected performance of the chosen solution.- Manufacture and test a prototype and evaluate the performance in a representative laboratory environment.Procurement Policy: C(1) = Activity restricted to non-prime contractors (incl. original.description: ESA operates one of the world's largest Earth Observation (EO) data archives, with data from missions dating back to the mid 1970s.Preserving these datatogether with the information and tools needed to interpret and use themis essential to analyse long-term environmental changes and support future decision-making. Beyond preservation and access, heritage data must be curated and improved to ensure continuity and comparability with newer missions. original.description: ObjectivesAssess the feasibility of using physics-based granular dynamics simulation to model the formation of cryovolcanic terrains on Enceladus and derive insights into surface compactness. Develop a proof-of-concept ML model for inferring snow/ice geophysicalproperties (e.g., density, snow water equivalent) by correlating terrestrial in-situ scientific data with satellite remote sensing observations. Initiate the adaptation of classical, optimization-based HDA frameworks to integrate AIderived geophysical safety maps, establishing a baseline for a future hybrid HDA architecture. Conduct an extensive performance and resource consumption benchmark of key AI and HDA software components on representative space-grade hardware, establishing the trade-space between algorithmic capability and on-board computational budgetDescriptionThe ESA Voyage 2050 L4 mission to Enceladus requires an autonomous landing in the South Polar Terrain to achieve its core astrobiological objectives. This environment presents unique challenges that transcend classical HDA capabilities. Landing hazardsare not only geometric (e.g., slopes, rocks), but also geophysical. Due to the unknown load-bearing capacity of cryovolcanic surface deposits, landing sites can appear perfectly flat and clear of hazards and yet be catastrophically unsafe. Classical existing Hazard Detection and Avoidance (HDA) frameworks targeting Moon and Mars, are highly mature for geometric hazard assessment but are not designed to infer subsurface geophysical properties from remote sensing data. This activity shall address this critical technology gap by investigating the integration of AI/ML-based geophysicalinference into a proven HDA decision-making architecture. Additionally, the severe power and computational constraints of a solar-powered missionto Saturn imposea hard limit on the complexity of on-board AI. It is currently unknown what level of "intelligence" is achievable within a realistic resource budget. This activity shall perform the foundational trade-off analysis required to inform mission designers of the necessary hardware and power provisions for a reliable and capable AI-augmented HDA system

description: ObjectivesAssess the feasibility of using physics-based granular dynamics simulation to model the formation of cryovolcanic terrains on Enceladus and derive insights into surface compactness. Develop a proof-of-concept ML model for inferring snow/ice geophysicalproperties (e.g., density, snow water equivalent) by correlating terrestrial in-situ scientific data with satellite remote sensing observations. Initiate the adaptation of classical, optimization-based HDA frameworks to integrate AIderived geophysical safety maps, establishing a baseline for a future hybrid HDA architecture. Conduct an extensive performance and resource consumption benchmark of key AI and HDA software components on representative space-grade hardware, establishing the trade-space between algorithmic capability and on-board computational budgetDescriptionThe ESA Voyage 2050 L4 mission to Enceladus requires an autonomous landing in the South Polar Terrain to achieve its core astrobiological objectives. This environment presents unique challenges that transcend classical HDA capabilities. Landing hazardsare not only geometric (e.g., slopes, rocks), but also geophysical. Due to the unknown load-bearing capacity of cryovolcanic surface deposits, landing sites can appear perfectly flat and clear of hazards and yet be catastrophically unsafe. Classical existing Hazard Detection and Avoidance (HDA) frameworks targeting Moon and Mars, are highly mature for geometric hazard assessment but are not designed to infer subsurface geophysical properties from remote sensing data. This activity shall address this critical technology gap by investigating the integration of AI/ML-based geophysicalinference into a proven HDA decision-making architecture. Additionally, the severe power and computational constraints of a solar-powered missionto Saturn imposea hard limit on the complexity of on-board AI. It is currently unknown what level of "intelligence" is achievable within a realistic resource budget. This activity shall perform the foundational trade-off analysis required to inform mission designers of the necessary hardware and power provisions for a reliable and capable AI-augmented HDA system
